```{r}
#| label: library
#| include: false
options(housepi.footer.warranty = TRUE)
options(housepi.footer.sample = TRUE)
library(housepi)
housepi_theme_set()
```

In this vignette we show how to compute common household measures according to the model posterior distribution. This is generally referred to as Posterior Predictive Checks (PPC). We use the same chain binomial example presented in [Get started](housepi.html):

```{r}
#| label: inference-setup
# repeat inference as in vignette 'Get Started'
set.seed(42)
hhmodel <- new_housepi_model(flu_1918_frederick, "chain_binomial") |>
  add_parameter_template()

# estimate parameters
results <- hhmodel |>
  run_inference(steps = 2000, thin = 10, burn = 500, adapt = 500, chains = 4)
estimates <- get_param_draws(results) |>
  posterior::summarise_draws()
estimates
```

# Predicted cases by size

We can use the simulation process to challenge the validity of the inferred model on top of the original dataset. We do so by computing the predicted numbers of cases per household size according to our posterior distribution (i.e. by producing simulations according to posterior values).

```{r}
#| label: compute-predictions
# compute posterior predictive checks
ppc <- hhmodel |>
  # run simulations according to previous posterior traces in results
  predicted_cases_by_house_size(results)
```

To show both observed and predicted cases by size, we can extract the formatted cases table from our output object as follows.

```{r}
#| label: format-cases-table
# for this part of the analysis we consider only house sizes up to 5
ppc$set_max_house_size(5)

# return a data.frame with observed and predicted cases
cases_df <- ppc$formatted_cases_table

# format predicted cases
combined <- cases_df$mean
mask_pred <- cases_df$mean$distr == "Predicted"
mask_cols <- setdiff(names(cases_df$mean), c("house_size", "distr"))

# format mean with its lower and upper credible interval bounds
combined[mask_pred, mask_cols] <- format_credible_intervals(
  cases_df$mean[mask_pred, mask_cols],
  cases_df$q5[mask_pred, mask_cols],
  cases_df$q95[mask_pred, mask_cols],
  as_integer = TRUE
)

# avoid separate_header regular expression to split house_size
names(combined)[names(combined) == "house_size"] <- "size"

# generate cases by household size table
flextable::flextable(combined) |>
  flextable::separate_header() |>
  flextable::bold(j = ~ size, bold = TRUE) |>
  flextable::merge_v(j = ~ size) |>
  flextable::align(align = "center", , part = "all") |>
  flextable::labelizor(labels = c(size = "Size",
                                  distr = "Distribution",
                                  cases = "Number of Cases")) |>
  flextable::autofit()
```

We can perform a Chi-Squared test on the shown distribution as follows:

```{r}
#| label: chisq-test
# perform a Chi-Squared test
ppc$chisq_test()
```

The $p$-value tells us that there is no significant difference between the distributions ($p > 0.05$), thus we can trust our inference process.

# Secondary attack rate

We can have a quick look at secondary attack rates of observed vs predicted cases using the field `$sar`:

```{r}
#| label: sar-plot
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Secondary attack rates by household size comparing posterior estimates (orange) with observed data (black points with sample sizes).
#|  Predicted values show mean posterior estimates with 95% credible intervals, stratified by household size from 2 to 7 members.

# we drop maximum house size before proceeding
ppc$drop_max_house_size()

library(ggplot2)

col_dict <- c(Predicted = "coral", Observed = "black")

# extract values for secondary attack rate
ggplot(ppc$formatted_sec_attack_rate,
       aes(x = as.factor(house_size), y = observed, 
           label = sprintf("[%s]", counts))) +
  # predicted SAR
  geom_point(aes(y = mean, color = "Predicted")) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(y = mean, ymin = q5, ymax = q95, color = "Predicted")) +
  # observed SAR
  geom_point(aes(color = "Observed")) +
  # annotate observed counts
  geom_text(nudge_x = 0.3, color = col_dict["Observed"]) +
  scale_color_manual(values = col_dict) +
  labs(x = "Household Size", y = "Secondary Attack Rate", color = "")
```

# Other posterior measures

The `predicted_measures()` function provides a flexible way to compute any custom measure on simulated data and compare it against the observed values. 
It accepts one or more named measure functions as arguments, where each function takes a `data_wide` data.frame and returns a summary as a data.frame, a numeric vector or other.

You can also pass multiple custom measures at once, eventually alongside the built-in measure functions otherwise embedded in `predicted_cases_by_house_size`. 
Current built-in measure are

-   `measure_sar_by_house_size`: secondary attack rate by household size;
-   `measure_cases_by_house_size`: contingency table of cases by household size.

A custom measure function should accept a `data_wide` data.frame and return a `data.frame`, a `list`, or a `numeric` vector:
  
```{r}
#| label: predicted-measures-custom
# define a custom measure: overall attack rate
measure_overall_attack_rate <- function(data_wide) {
  sum(data_wide$status > 0, na.rm = TRUE) / nrow(data_wide)
}

# compute both built-in and custom measures together
ppc_multi <- hhmodel |>
  predicted_measures(results,
                     sar = measure_sar_by_house_size,
                     overall = measure_overall_attack_rate)
ppc_multi
```

The returned `HousepiPrediction` object stores `observed`, `predicted`, `cri_lower` and `cri_upper` for each measure, accessible by name:
  
```{r}
#| label: extract-sar-components
# bind observed secondary attack rates
ppc_multi$sar$observed |> 
  # to predicted (posterior mean) values
  dplyr::left_join(ppc_multi$sar$predicted, by = "house_size", 
                   suffix = c("_observed", "_predicted"))
```

Similarly can be done for all stored measures:

```{r}
#| label: plot-overall-attack-rate
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 2.5
#| fig-alt: >
#|  Overall attack rates comparison between observed and predicted.
#|  Predicted mean value shown with errorbars for the 95% credible interval
# compare observed vs predicted overall attack rate
ggplot(data.frame(ppc_multi$overall)) +
  geom_point(aes(x = "observed", y = observed), color = "black") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(x = "predicted", y = observed,
                    ymin = cri_lower, ymax = cri_upper)) + 
  geom_point(aes(x = "predicted", y = predicted)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Attack rate")

```
